subject: Louis XIV of France
overview: Louis XIV became king of France at the age of four and reigned for 72 years, longer than any other monarch of a major European country. He ruled without a chief minister, turned a hunting lodge at Versailles into a vast palace where the nobility lived under his eye, and fought a long series of wars that pushed France's borders outward. He also revoked the toleration of French Protestants, and when he died in 1715 the throne passed to his five-year-old great-grandson.

key_moments.title: Child king and the Fronde
key_moments.text: When **Louis XIII** died in 1643, his son was only four, so his mother **Anne of Austria** governed as regent with **Cardinal Mazarin** running the government. Taxes and resentment of Mazarin sparked the **Fronde**, a string of revolts by the Paris parlement and great nobles that lasted from 1648 to 1653. In January 1649 the royal family **slipped out of Paris at night** to escape the unrest. The boy never forgot the humiliation, and it helps explain why the adult king later kept his nobles close and **moved his court out of Paris**.
claims: Louis XIV became King of France in 1643 at the age of four after the death of Louis XIII.
Anne of Austria served as regent for Louis XIV, with Cardinal Mazarin as chief minister.
The Fronde was a series of revolts in France lasting from 1648 to 1653.
In January 1649 the French royal family fled Paris at night during the Fronde.

key_moments.title: Personal rule and the fall of Fouquet
key_moments.text: When **Mazarin died in 1661**, the 22-year-old Louis announced that he would govern without a chief minister. That summer his finance superintendent **Nicolas Fouquet** threw a lavish fête for him at his new château of **Vaux-le-Vicomte**. Weeks later, in September 1661, Fouquet was **arrested by d'Artagnan**, the musketeer officer later made famous by Dumas, and spent the rest of his life in prison. The king then hired the architect, painter and garden designer of Vaux, **Le Vau, Le Brun and Le Nôtre**, to work on Versailles.
claims: Cardinal Mazarin died in 1661.
After Mazarin's death in 1661, Louis XIV ruled without appointing a chief minister.
Nicolas Fouquet held a lavish fête for Louis XIV at Vaux-le-Vicomte in August 1661.
Nicolas Fouquet was arrested in September 1661 by d'Artagnan and remained imprisoned until his death.
Louis Le Vau, Charles Le Brun and André Le Nôtre, who had worked on Vaux-le-Vicomte, went on to work on the Palace of Versailles.

key_moments.title: The court moves to Versailles
key_moments.text: After years of building, Louis made the **Palace of Versailles** the official seat of the court and government in **1682**. Thousands of courtiers lived there, and great nobles who once raised armies against the crown now competed for the honour of handing the king his shirt during the morning **lever** ceremony. The palace's **Hall of Mirrors** became a showcase of French wealth and craftsmanship. Versailles was copied by rulers across Europe, and the system kept the aristocracy busy with rank and etiquette instead of rebellion.
claims: Louis XIV moved the French royal court and government to the Palace of Versailles in 1682.
Louis XIV's daily routine at Versailles included a public rising ceremony called the lever, attended by courtiers.
The Hall of Mirrors is part of the Palace of Versailles built under Louis XIV.
Louis XIV's court at Versailles drew the French nobility away from their provincial power bases.

key_moments.title: Revoking the Edict of Nantes
key_moments.text: With the **Edict of Fontainebleau** in 1685, Louis revoked the **Edict of Nantes**, the 1598 law that had given French Protestants, the **Huguenots**, legal toleration. Protestant churches were destroyed and pastors were ordered to leave, while ordinary Protestants were forbidden to emigrate. Many left anyway; an estimated 200,000 or more fled to places such as the Dutch Republic, England, Switzerland and Brandenburg-Prussia. Their crafts and trades went with them, and **Brandenburg actively invited them in**, strengthening one of France's future rivals.
claims: Louis XIV issued the Edict of Fontainebleau in 1685, revoking the Edict of Nantes.
The Edict of Nantes of 1598 had granted legal toleration to French Protestants.
The Edict of Fontainebleau ordered Protestant pastors to leave France while forbidding other Protestants to emigrate.
An estimated 200,000 or more Huguenots left France after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes.
Brandenburg issued the Edict of Potsdam in 1685 inviting Huguenot refugees to settle.

deep_facts.text: The "Sun King" image started on a stage. In 1653, at fourteen, Louis danced in the **Ballet Royal de la Nuit**, a performance lasting many hours that ended at dawn with the young king appearing as the rising sun in a costume of gold. He kept dancing in court ballets for years, and in 1661 he founded the **Académie Royale de Danse**. Much of the vocabulary of classical ballet, including its French terms, grew out of the dance culture of his court.
claims: Louis XIV danced in the Ballet Royal de la Nuit in 1653.
In the Ballet Royal de la Nuit, Louis XIV appeared as the rising sun.
Louis XIV founded the Académie Royale de Danse in 1661.
Classical ballet terminology is in French because ballet was codified at the French court.

deep_facts.text: In 1686 the king underwent risky surgery for an **anal fistula**, performed by the surgeon **Charles-François Félix**. He recovered, and celebrations followed across France. The next year his court composer **Jean-Baptiste Lully** conducted a Te Deum honouring the king's recovery, beating time by striking the floor with a long staff. He hit his own foot, the wound turned gangrenous, he refused amputation, and he died weeks later in 1687: a composer killed by a celebration of his patron's health.
claims: Louis XIV underwent surgery for an anal fistula in 1686.
The surgeon Charles-François Félix operated on Louis XIV's fistula.
Jean-Baptiste Lully struck his foot with his conducting staff while conducting a Te Deum celebrating Louis XIV's recovery.
Jean-Baptiste Lully refused amputation of his gangrenous foot and died in 1687.

deep_facts.text: Louis lived so long that his heirs ran out. His only surviving legitimate son, the **Grand Dauphin**, died in 1711. In 1712 measles killed the next heir, the **Duke of Burgundy**, his wife and their elder son within weeks of each other. The two-year-old who survived, reportedly because his governess **Madame de Ventadour** kept the doctors away from him, became **Louis XV** in 1715: a great-grandson succeeding his great-grandfather.
claims: Louis, Grand Dauphin, the son of Louis XIV, died in 1711.
Louis, Duke of Burgundy, his wife Marie Adélaïde of Savoy and their elder son died of measles in 1712.
The future Louis XV reportedly survived the 1712 measles outbreak because his governess Madame de Ventadour kept the doctors away from him.
Louis XV, the great-grandson of Louis XIV, became king in 1715.

connections.name: Cardinal Mazarin
connections.connection: Ran France as chief minister during Louis's minority and taught him statecraft until his death in 1661.

connections.name: Anne of Austria
connections.connection: His mother, who ruled as regent from 1643 while he was a child.

connections.name: Jean-Baptiste Colbert
connections.connection: His finance minister from the 1660s, who replaced Fouquet and reorganised France's trade and finances.

connections.name: War of the Spanish Succession
connections.connection: His last and largest war, fought from 1701 to secure the Spanish throne for his grandson.

connections.name: Philip V of Spain
connections.connection: His grandson, who became King of Spain in 1700 and kept the throne after the War of the Spanish Succession.

connections.name: Louis XV
connections.connection: His great-grandson, who succeeded him at the age of five in 1715.

connections.name: William III of England
connections.connection: His leading opponent, who organised coalitions against France from the Dutch Republic and later from England.

connections.name: Nine Years' War
connections.connection: Fought from 1688 against a broad European coalition seeking to contain his expansion.

connections.name: Maria Theresa of Spain
connections.connection: His queen, married in 1660 under the Peace of the Pyrenees; her Spanish lineage underpinned later French claims to Spain.

connections.name: Jean-Baptiste Lully
connections.connection: His court composer, who wrote the ballets and operas performed for him and danced alongside him.
